text.text: Previous research has established that war negatively impacts dreaming whereas findings on the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic are less consistent.
According to the Threat simulation theory (TST), dreams constitute an evolutionary adaptation where threatening situations are rehearsed.
Dreams are specialized in simulating threats that were most relevant in the human ancestral environment.

Since interpersonal physical aggression was a more salient threat compared to epidemics in the ancestral environment, with a direct behavioral response, TST predicts a greater elevation of threatening dream content in response to the Russo-Ukrainian war than to the COVID-19 pandemic.

To test this, we compared two Finnish prospective dream diary samples: 567 dreams from 45 participants collected after the beginning of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine to 1128 dreams from 85 participants collected in an identical design during the harshest COVID-19 restrictions.

The Russo-Ukrainian war elevated threatening dream content more than the COVID-19 pandemic, especially threats related to physical aggression, despite the fact that the war was experienced only through media in Finland.
In addition, dreams with direct references to warfare had more threats and more threats related to physical aggression compared to dreams without references to warfare.
Contrary to expectations, the severity of dream threats was not significantly different in these samples.
Individual dispositional factors predicted threats and threats related to warfare in dreams better than daily-measured situational factors.
This indicates that threatening dream content is better predicted by stable trait-like psychological disposition than a dynamic response to daily fluctuating situational variables.
Even though Russia occupied the Crimean Peninsula and eastern parts of Ukraine already in 2014, the full-scale invasion in February 2022 was a shock to Europe.
Finnish people were especially taken aback due to the long and difficult history with Russia.
Two years before the invasion, another large-scale threat, the COVID-19 pandemic, had hit globally.
Both of these events not only affected the waking lives of people, but their sleep and dreams as well.
Many studies have documented the negative effect the pandemic had on the mental health and dreaming of the general population.
The pandemic increased dream recall and negatively toned dreams, especially in women and in people who were most affected by the pandemic.

These studies were, however, mostly conducted with retrospective measures using questionnaires about dreaming or the most-recent-dream-method, where participants are asked to report the most recent dream they can remember.

Studies using systematic prospective measures, mainly dream diary studies, did not provide evidence of such a large negative effect on dream content, but rather found that only a small subset of dreams included pandemic content.
The effect of war on dreams is also a well-documented phenomenon.

For example, experiencing war increases dream recall, nightmares, and threatening events in dreams, induces more negative and decreases positive emotions in dreams, and is associated with higher PTSD symptom severity, with effects being more pronounced among individuals who are more affected by war.
Some of these same effects are seen also in people impacted by the Russo-Ukrainian war.
War-related dream imagery is predicted by exposure to war, war-related PTSD, fear of war, and is associated with insomnia.

In one study of Polish Auschwitz survivors, war-related dream imagery was more common in dreams after the war compared to dreams dreamt during the war, although a limitation was that the sample consisted of dreams reported 30 years after the war ended.

In war veterans, especially those with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), war-related posttraumatic nightmares 1, 2 314 415 1618 1927 28,2 9 28,3032 2 0 often depict elements of a specific moment of violence that the dreamer has experienced in waking life.

The threat simulation theory of dreaming (TST) defines dreams as offline simulations where we rehearse perceiving, recognizing, and coping with threatening events so we can react to them more appropriately in waking life.

This nocturnal rehearsal increased the fitness of ancestral humans via more effective threat perception, and avoidance and coping responses, and was therefore selected for in the course of human evolution.
A core prediction of TST is that real-world threat exposure activates the threat simulation system most profoundly, increasing the frequency and intensity of threatening dream content.

But real-world threats come in many forms, and threats that were most salient in the ancestral environment are a stronger trigger to activate the threat simulation system compared to more modern threats that did not exist in a concrete manner in the ancestral world.

According to TST, physical aggression is a more prevalent threat in dreams than infectious diseases, because physical aggression was a more salient threat in the waking lives of our ancestors, with easy-to-understand and implementable direct behavioral responses, than an epidemic or pandemic.

Viruses, bacteria, and other microscopic pathogens are invisible threats that could not have been physically confronted or easily avoided in the environment of evolutionary adaptedness, though we have a natural disgust and avoidance reaction to individuals displaying symptoms of illnesses.
Regardless, an effective threat rehearsal mechanism should focus on training for situations that are most critical in waking life and can be behaviorally trained for.

Loukola et al. and Domhoff discovered that the pandemic was featured only in a small percentage of dreams in systematic dream diaries, and that the pandemic did not significantly increase threatening dream content.

The threat simulation mechanism seemed to incorporate some pandemic content but did not produce frequent threat simulations involving infectious diseases, social isolation, or other pandemic-related issues.
War exposure or threat of war, however, represent a concrete, physical threat more closely resembling the hostile ancestral environments TST was 3 3 3 4 3 5 1 6 1 8 shaped to respond to.

Consequently, TST would predict that war should produce particularly robust activation of the threat simulation system, especially among those with personal exposure or close geographical proximity to the conflict.
Previous research has shown that trauma caused by interpersonal violence produces more trauma-related nightmares than non-interpersonal trauma.
Finnish people are not geographically close to the conflict but the Russo-Ukrainian war was and still is very widely represented and discussed in the Finnish media.
Exposure to threatening content via media has been associated with higher levels of threatening dream content.

Further, individual factors, such as belonging to the military reserve (to which approximately 900 000 Finns, ~50% of males aged between 18-60 years, belong to) or vulnerability to anxiety, may play a role in how easily the threat simulation system is activated by a close-by military conflict.

TST predicts that both daily fluctuating situational factors (e.g., daily stress) and more stable situational factors (e.g., personality traits) have an effect on the activation levels of the threat simulation system.
Empirical research supports the effects of both situational and individual factors on threatening dream content.
For example, waking-life experiences affect threatening dream content, posttraumatic dreams being the most extreme version.
Less intense experiences, like stress and rumination on anxious thoughts, seem to alter threatening dream content as well.
Consumption of media related to a threatening event has also been linked to increased threat levels in dreams.
In previous research, neuroticism, hyperarousal, and impaired fear extinction due to traumatic experiences and childhood adversity seem to increase nightmare frequency.

Even though there are numerous studies on the effect of war on sleep and dream content, there is a shortage of research on individual and situational factors that predict war-related dream content other than factors that relate directly to war (e.g., exposure to war).

In our previous study on the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on threatening dream content, lower life satisfaction predicted threatening dream content and lower positive emotions in the past two weeks pandemic-related threatening events.
In addition, stable and enduring individual factors had higher 3638 39,4 0 4 1 4 2 19,4 3 44,4 5 41,4 6 47,4 8 4 9 variable importance than situational factors that fluctuated day-to-day.
This indicates that more stable features may predict dream content better than daily fluctuating mental states, even in the face of an adversity such as threat of war.
Previous research seems to also point in this direction, even though mostly done on nightmares, and conflicting results also exist.
We suggest that relatively stable individual factors modulate the impact of situational factors on dream content.

The aim of the present study was to examine, in two Finnish dream diary samples, whether the Russo-Ukrainian war increased the frequency or severity of threatening dream content compared to the COVID-19 pandemic, as predicted by TST.
The predictors of threatening events, and especially threatening events related to warfare, were also examined.
All the hypotheses and analyses were preregistered and can be found on the project's Open Science Framework webpage (https://osf.io/btvne/overview).
text.formatted: All the hypotheses and analyses were preregistered and can be found on the project's Open Science Framework webpage (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/btvne/overview">https://osf.io/btvne/</ref>).

text.text: This study addresses the following hypotheses: The Russo-Ukrainian war increased the number of threatening events (H1), the number of threatening events related to physical aggression (H2), and the relative number of severe to minor threats (H3) in dreams compared to dreams during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The dreams in the wartime sample that contain direct references to warfare have a higher number of threatening events (H4), a higher number of threats related to physical aggression (H5), and higher ratio of severe to minor threats (H6) than dreams without references to warfare.

Greater number of threatening situations (H7) and warfare-related threatening situations (H8) in dreams is associated with the following individual factors: belonging to military reserve, a close person belonging to military reserve, lower life satisfaction, greater amount of negative and lower amount of positive emotions in the last two weeks, lower peace of mind, and greater amount of anxiety and depression symptoms in the last two weeks.

Similarly, greater number of threatening situations (H7) and warfare-related threatening situations (H8) is 5054 55,5 associated with the following situational factors: greater amount of negative emotions and lower amount of positive emotions during a mind-wandering task the previous evening, greater amount of negative and lower amount of positive emotions during the previous day, greater amount of worry related to the Russo-Ukrainian war experienced during the previous day, and greater amount of media consumption related to the Russo-Ukrainian war during the previous day.
For the war sample, 89 participants submitted 748 dream reports and 596 mind-wandering reports.
For the pandemic sample, 297 participants submitted 1534 dream reports and 1251 mind-wandering reports.
In this study, we utilized data only from participants who provided at least five dream and mind-wandering reports.

This left us with 45 participants (8 men, 36 women, 1 "don't want to tell"; M = 48.58 years, SD = 13.96, range = 23 -71) providing 567 dream reports (M = 12.60, SD = 6.21) in the war sample, and 85 participants (4 men, 78 women, and 3 others; M = 37.71 years, SD = 15.98, range = 19-73) providing 1128 dream reports (M = 13.3, SD = 6.9) in the pandemic sample.
Mind-wandering reports are not utilized in this study.
When testing hypotheses concerning situational factors (H7 & H8), we excluded participants who had fewer than 3 consecutive mindwandering and dream reports.
text.formatted: When testing hypotheses concerning situational factors (H7 & H8), we excluded participants who had fewer than 3 consecutive mindwandering and dream reports.

text.text: Both the Russo-Ukrainian war sample (war sample, or just the sample) and the COVID-19 sample (pandemic sample) were collected through identical methods.

For the war sample, the "Russo-Ukrainian War in our minds", and for the pandemic sample, the "COVID-19 in our minds", studies were advertised through the student societies' email lists of almost all the major Finnish universities.
The studies were also advertised on social media, and they gained some mainstream media exposure, which helped to recruit participants from the general population.
The studies were advertised to investigate the contents of dreaming and mind-wandering during these extraordinary times.

People interested in participating in the studies were directed to the studies' websites where more information about the studies was shared, with instructions on how to effectively keep a dream journal and how to do the daily mind-wandering task.
From these websites, the participants also received their unique study IDs to be able to participate anonymously.
The personal study ID enabled connecting different dream reports, mind-wandering reports, and other daily measurements to the same participant.

After providing informed consent and affirming to be at least 18 years old, the participants were requested to fill in information about their age, gender, living arrangement (alone, with a partner, with family, with a friend/roommate), whether they or a close one had completed the compulsory military service in Finland (war sample), or whether they or a close one belonged to the COVID-19 risk group (pandemic sample).

Then, the participants filled out questionnaires about well-being, attitudes towards other people, and personality (detailed measures are reported under Materials: Independent variables: individual factors).
After finishing the survey, the participants kept a dream journal and did a mindwandering task every evening for two weeks.
For the dream diary, the participants were asked to report all the dreams that they had the previous night without adding or subtracting anything.
The participants were to write down all the dreams immediately after waking up and submit them online.

With every dream report the participants reported the time they woke up, how much positive and negative emotions they experienced during the dream, whether the dream was a nightmare or a lucid dream (war sample only), sleep quality during the night (war sample only), and with how many people they had been in contact with face-to-face, or through video calls (war sample only), or via traditional phone calls (war sample only) during the previous day.
The other daily task for the participants was to carry out a 10-minute mind-wandering task every evening.
The participants were instructed to sit still and let their minds wander freely.
After the 10 minutes, the participants were to write down everything that went through their minds during the task without adding or subtracting anything.

Additionally, the participants were to report the time when they did the task, how much positive or negative emotions they experienced during the task, how much the Russo-Ukrainian war (war sample only) or COVID-19 (pandemic sample only) had worried them during the day, how much they had followed media related to the Russo-Ukrainian war (war sample only) or COVID-19 (pandemic sample only) during the day, and whether they or a close one had been infected with COVID-19 (pandemic sample only).
The participants also filled out a Positive Negative Affect Scale (PANAS) about their emotions during the day.
All the reporting in the study was done anonymously via Webropol online forms (new.webropolsurveys.com).
Because all the data was collected anonymously, no ethical approval was needed for the study according to the TENK (Finnish national board on research integrity) guidelines.
The participants had the option to quit the study at any moment for any reason.
The dreams in both samples were manually rated using the Dream Threat Scale (DTS), a content analysis tool to identify and categorize threatening events from written reports.
The analyses were done in two stages by three independent raters.
The order of the dreams in each sample was randomized, and participant IDs were removed for the analyses so the raters did not know which dreams belonged to which participant.
In the first stage, the raters identified all threatening events.
A threatening event is defined as an event in the dream that would in real life compromise any person's well-being or their resources.
The event can be directly witnessed by the dreamer or it can The categorizations agreed upon by at least two out of the three raters were included in the statistical analyses.
In this study, the categories of interest are the Nature of the Threatening Event and the Severity of the Threatening Event for the Self.
Descriptive statistics (N, %) for the remaining categories can be found in the supplementary material (Tables S1-S4).
text.formatted: Descriptive statistics (N, %) for the remaining categories can be found in the supplementary material (Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">S1-S4</ref>).

text.text: While identifying the threatening events, the raters also identified whether the dream had references to warfare.

The references could be, for example, armed conflicts, warfare-related equipment (e.g., tanks, guns), warfare-related constructions and buildings (e.g., trenches), or people related to the Russo-Ukrainian war familiar from media (e.g., presidents of Ukraine or Russia, war analysts).

Additionally, researchers V.L. and K.V. distinguished warfare-related and non-warfarerelated threatening events from the dreams that at least two out of the three raters had identified to have references to warfare, with disagreements resolved through discussion.
Individual factors were measured once at the beginning of the study in the questionnaire.

The individual factors of interest in the current study were: belonging to a military reserve, a close person belonging to a military reserve, life satisfaction, negative emotions in the past two weeks, positive emotions in the past two weeks, peace of mind, anxiety symptoms in the past two weeks, and depression symptoms in the past two weeks.
a The pandemic sample was categorized using an older version of DTS, where the possibility to participate in and the reaction to the threatening event were separate categories.
Yet, the same information can be extracted from the older and newer versions of the scale.
Belonging to the military reserve was measured with a yes/no question: "Have you completed military service in Finland?"
(11.1% responded "yes", n = 5).
A close person belonging to a military reserve was measured with a yes/no question: "Has your close one completed military service in Finland?"
(68.9% responded "yes", n = 31).
Life satisfaction was measured with the 5 9 6 0 5 7 5 7 6 1 6 1 6 2 6 3 6 4 6 5
Situational factors were measured daily in conjunction with the mind-wandering task.

The individual factors of interest in the current study were: negative and positive emotions during a mind-wandering task, negative and positive emotions during the day, worry related to the Russo-Ukrainian war experienced during the day, and media consumption related to the Russo-Ukrainian war during the day.
Negative and positive emotions during the mind-wandering task were measured with a 5-point scale ranging from "none" to "very much".
Negative and positive emotions during the day were measured with Positive and Negative Affect Schedule.
The sample means were close to the general population's means.
Worry related to the Russo-Ukrainian war during the day was measured with a question: "How much has the war in Ukraine worried you today?"
with a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "not at all" to "very much".
Media consumption related to the Russo-Ukrainian war during the day was measured with a question: "How much have you followed news related to the war in Ukraine?"
with a 5-point scale ranging from "not at all" to "over 3 hours".
Generalized linear mixed-effects models were built to test all the hypotheses using the glmmTMB package in R statistical software (version 4.4.0).
We used glmmTMB over the more popular lme4 package because around half of the dreams contain no threats, and glmmTMB handels zeroinflated data more effectively.
A separate model was built for every hypothesis.
Age and gender were controlled by adding them as fixed effects into the models, because previous research has shown that younger people and women tend to have more emotionally negative dreams.
Age was scaled, and gender was deviation coded.

For H3 and H6, all threats that were categorized as 5 7 66,6 7 1 6 6 6 8 physically, socially, psychologically, or financially severe or life-threatening were combined to comprise a variable severe threats.
For H7 and H8, all the categorized variables used in the models were deviation-coded, and all the continuous variables were centered.
Maximal random effect structure (that converges) was used and participants were fitted as random intercepts.
DHARMa package was used to test zero-inflation and overdispersion.
Because precise p-values are hard to determine from generalized linear mixed-effects models, the statistical significance of p < .05 is indicated by values of z > |1.96|.
text.formatted: Because precise p-values are hard to determine from generalized linear mixed-effects models, the statistical significance of p < .05 is indicated by values of z > |1.96|.

text.text: The complete models are reported in Tables S5-S13 in the supplementary material.
text.formatted: The complete models are reported in Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">S5</ref>-S13 in the supplementary material.

text.text: Regarding H7 and H8, many of the individual and situational variables correlated with each other (see Table S14).
text.formatted: Regarding H7 and H8, many of the individual and situational variables correlated with each other (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">S14</ref>).

text.text: All the variables could not be inserted into the same model because of collinearity issues.
However, building separate models for each variable would have significantly raised the possibility of type 1 error.
Further, previous literature did not give us any strong rationale to pick some variables over others.
In addition, TST predicts that both individual and situational variables influence threatening dream content.
To mitigate this issue, random forest analyses were used both in testing H7 and H8 to determine the variables used in the mixed effects models.

Random forest analysis is a non-parametric technique to determine variables with the highest importance when predicting an outcome variable, which are 'threatening events in dreams' (H7) and 'warfare-related threatening events in dreams' (H8).
The variables with the highest variable importance were chosen.
From the random forest plot, a cut-off point for chosen variables was visually determined and marked with a horizontal line (Figures 1 2 3).
text.formatted: From the random forest plot, a cut-off point for chosen variables was visually determined and marked with a horizontal line (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref> <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">2</ref> <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">3</ref>).

text.text: Random forest analysis does not determine statistical significance or the direction of the effect, and was thus used to provide an objective way to determine the variables that would be later tested with generalized linear mixed-effects models.

To ensure a representative sample from each participant, all participants who failed to provide at least three consecutive mind-wandering and dream reports were excluded from the random forest analyses.

Therefore, the final sample for the random forest analyses was 42 participants (7 men, 34 women, 1 "don't want to tell"; M = 49.6, SD = 13.7, range = 23 -71) who submitted 536 dreams (M = 12.8, SD = 6.4).
The excluded participants were later included in the mixed-effects models because these can handle missing data better.

Generative AI (ChatGPT 5.5 and 5.6) was used in troubleshooting existing R code when statistical assumptions of the analyses were not met, and in assisting in creating Excel formulas for more efficient data handling.
The data and the R code were reviewed by the authors and all the statistical interpretations were done by the authors.
In the war sample, there were a total of 639 threats in 567 dreams (M = 1.13 threats per dream, SD = 1.61).
In the pandemic sample, there were 998 threats in 1128 dreams (M = 0.88 threats per dream, SD = 1.06).
In the war sample, 251 dreams (37.7%) and in the pandemic sample, 507 dreams (44.9%) did not contain any threats.

The model for the number of threatening events revealed a difference between the war and pandemic samples, β = 0.27, 95% CI [0.02, 0.52], z = 2.10, indicating that the war sample had more threatening events in dreams compared to the pandemic sample.
The frequencies for the Nature of the Threatening Event category are shown in Table 1.

text.text: In the war sample, there were 134 threats (20.9%), and in the pandemic sample, 149 threats (14.9%) related to physical aggression.

The model for the number of threats related to physical aggression revealed a difference between the war and pandemic samples, β = 0.55, 95% CI [0.18, 0.93], z = 2.93, indicating that the war sample had more threats related to physical aggression than the pandemic sample.
The frequencies for the Severity of the Threat category are shown in Table 2.

The model for the relative number of severe threats to minor threats did not reveal a difference between the war and pandemic samples, β = 0.19, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.51], z = 1.13.
In the war sample, there were 98 dreams with direct references to warfare (17.3%), and 469 dreams without direct references to warfare (82.7%).
The dreams with direct references to warfare included 151 threats (M = 1.54 threats per dream, SD = 1.77), while in 27 dreams there were no threats (27.6%).
The dreams without references to warfare included 488 threats (M = 1.04 threats per dream, SD = 1.57), and in 224 dreams there were no threats (47.8%).
The model for the number of threatening events revealed a difference between the dreams with and without direct references to warfare in the war sample, β = 0.43, 95% CI [0.16, 0.71], z = 3.07.
This indicates that the dreams with direct references to warfare had more threatening events compared to the dreams that did not have direct references to warfare.
The frequencies for the Nature of the Threatening Event category between dreams with and without references to warfare are shown in Table 3.

The model for the number of threats related to physical aggression revealed a difference between the dreams with and without references to warfare in the war sample, β = 1.02, 95% CI [0.18, 1.86], z = 2.38.
This indicates that the dreams with direct references to warfare had more threats related to physical aggression compared to the dreams that did not have direct references to warfare.

Random forest analysis identified peace of mind as the best predictor for warfare-related threatening events in dreams (Figure 2), and it was fitted to a model on predictors for warfare-related threatening events in dreams.

text.text: Peace of mind was not a significant predictor, β = -0.18, 95% CI

Random forest analysis identified life-satisfaction, peace of mind, negative emotions in the past two weeks, anxiety symptoms in the past two weeks, depression symptoms in the past two weeks, and positive emotions in the past two weeks as the best predictors for threatening events in dreams when the pandemic sample was also included (Figure 3).

text.text: These variables were fitted to a model on predictors for threatening events in dreams.
There was no multicollinearity problem with all VIFvalues being < 3.
text.formatted: There was no multicollinearity problem with all VIFvalues being < 3.

text.text: The model did not show any of the variables to be significant predictors.
However, age predicted threatening events in dreams, β = -0.16, 95% CI [-0.28, -0.04], z = -2.55, indicating that younger participants had more threatening events in dreams.

Four of the eight hypotheses were confirmed: There were more threatening events and threats related to physical aggression in dreams collected during the war compared to dreams collected during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Also, in the war sample, there were more threatening events and threats related to physical aggression in dreams with references to warfare compared to dreams without references to warfare.

Contrary to our expectations, the ratio of severe to minor threats did not differ between the war sample and the pandemic sample and, in the war sample, between dreams with and without references to warfare.
In addition, no significant individual or situational predictors for either threatening events or warfare-related threatening events in dreams were found.
The confirmation of hypotheses H1 and H2 lends support to TST, which predicts that war activates the threat simulation mechanism more effectively than a pandemic.
According to TST, threats most likely to be selected for simulation were those that were both highly salient and behaviorally actionable in the ancestral environment.

Physical aggression meets both criteria: it is immediately perceptible, elicits a defined behavioral repertoire (fight, flight, freezing), and rehearsing that repertoire plausibly improves survival outcomes.
Infectious disease, by contrast, is perceptually diffuse and offers no clear behavioral script other than avoiding people exhibiting symptoms of an illness.
TST therefore predicts that physical threat scenarios dominate dream content not because disease posed lesser danger, but because its simulation would have conferred no or lesser rehearsal advantage.
Simulation of how to react to infectious diseases was not as clear in the environment of ancestral humans as threat simulation related to physical aggression.
As evidenced here, war was incorporated into 17.3% of dreams in the war sample, and elevated the overall threatening dream content and especially threats related to physical aggression.
However, the ratio of severe to minor threats was similar in the war and pandemic samples.
Even though war activated the threat simulation mechanism in the Finnish participants to some extent, it did not result in overall more severe threat simulations.
This is possibly because of the low personal exposure to the war and lack of direct threat to life and well-being.
Personal exposure to military conflicts in children and adolescents has been previously shown to increase not only threat frequency but also threat severity in dreams.

In contrast, in the pandemic sample, 15.1% of the threats were related to diseases and medical problems whereas in only 5.4% in the war sample, which is close to samples collected before the pandemic.

Even though not statistically tested, it seems that the pandemic might have elevated the number of threats related to illness (see Table 1), which, in the war sample collected after the pandemic in 2022, has started to decrease closer to the pre-pandemic values.
text.formatted: Even though not statistically tested, it seems that the pandemic might have elevated the number of threats related to illness (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), which, in the war sample collected after the pandemic in 2022, has started to decrease closer to the pre-pandemic values.

text.text: The confirmation of H4 and H5, that is, that dreams with references to warfare have more threats and more threats related to physical aggression, also supports TST's stance on dreaming.
Dreams with these references can be interpreted as purposeful simulations of a threatening event.
Even though the ratio of severe to minor threats was not elevated (H6) in the dreams with references to warfare, these dreams had proportionally more life-threatening events.
In dreams with references to warfare, 23.7% of the threats were life-threatening vs.
8.1% in the dreams without references to warfare.
Thus, while in a binary severe vs. minor threat categorization the difference was not significant, there was a clear percentage elevation in the most severe types of threats.

Like in our previous study, all the relatively stable individual factors were more important predictors for both threatening events and warfare-related threatening events than fluctuating situational factors.
Threatening dream content, and maybe dream content generally, may be affected more by relatively stable characteristics of an individual's psyche.

This does not indicate that daily events and fluctuating mental states do not have an effect on threatening dream content but rather that the within-person variation is smaller than between-person variation.
Notably, we did not replicate the results of our previous study that life satisfaction, or any other factor selected via random forest analysis, was a significant predictor for threatening events.
Even when we combined the war and the pandemic samples to test for predictors of threatening events in dreams, the result remained unchanged.
This raises the question of why we found a significant predictor in the pandemic sample but not in the war sample.
Our results showed that the threat simulation mechanism is activated more during war, but possibly war also changes the way the threat simulation mechanism operates.
While the possibility that the results of our previous study reflected a false-positive finding cannot be entirely ruled out, differences between the samples provide a more plausible explanation.
Future studies are needed to clarify which variables most reliably predict threatening dream content.

Previous research has indicated that age would be a predictor for negatively toned dreams, and also in this study younger age predicted more threatening events and warfare-related threatening events in dreams.
The biggest strengths of the current study were the large sample sizes and identical data collection and analysis methods between samples.
In addition, both samples were collected when the crisis at hand was still very urgent and new, making the data collection very timely.
The number of male participants in both samples was, however, low, and the effects of gender could not be adequately studied.
Females have been shown to have more negatively toned dreams.

Also, due to the low number of male participants, we had only a few participants who were in the military reserve, and therefore the effect of being in the military reserve could not be adequately studied.

Overall, our large prospective dream diary samples collected during the early stages of the full-scale Russo-Ukrainian war and the harshest COVID-19 restrictions indicated that war elevates threatening dream content more profoundly compared to a pandemic.
This can be interpreted as support for the TST.

This study did not find significant predictors for threatening events or warfare-related threatening events in dreams, even though in the random forest analyses all the one-time measured individual factors had higher variable importance compared to daily measured situational factors.
Experiencing threatening dream content seems to behave in a similar manner to dispositional traits that remain relatively stable over time.
This does not remove the 76,7 7 1 0 effect of daily life on dream content, only that it has a lesser effect.
Further research should try to get more balanced gender distribution in the sample so the effect of gender on threatening dream content could be studied.

The threats identified by at least two out of the three raters qualified for the second stage, in which the three raters independently categorized the threats in the following categories: the Nature of the Threatening Event, the Target of the Threat, the Severity of the Threatening Event for the Self, the Possibility of Participating in and Reaction to the Threatening Event, Resolution of the Threat, and the Realistic Nature of the Threatening Event. a
Satisfaction with Life Scale.
The scores can vary between 5 and 35, with a higher number indicating greater life satisfaction.
The sample mean indicated "slightly satisfied" and was very close to the general population.
The negative and positive emotions in the past two weeks were measured with the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS).
The instructions for the participants were: "Evaluate how much you have experienced the following emotions in the past two weeks?"
The scores for both the positive and negative affect can vary between 10 and 50, with a smaller value indicating fewer emotions experienced.
The sample mean for positive affect was close to a general population mean, but negative affect was slightly elevated.
Peace of mind was measured with the Peace of Mind Scale.
The score can vary between 1 and 5, and a higher score indicates stronger peace of mind.
The sample mean was close to the average in Asian and American Taiwanese populations.
The anxiety symptoms in the past two weeks were measured with the Generalized Anxiety Disorder questionnaire (GAD-7).
The instructions for the participants were: "Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by the following problems?"
The overall score can vary between 0 and 21, with higher score indicating problems more often.
The sample mean was just over the "mild anxiety symptoms" (score 5) cut-off point and slightly higher than a German general population sample mean.
The depression symptoms in the past two weeks were measured with the depression part of the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9).
The instructions for the participants were: "Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by the following problems?"
The overall score can vary between 0 and 27, and a higher score indicates more depressive symptoms.
The sample mean was just over the "mild depressive symptoms" (score 5) cut-off point and was slightly higher than a German population sample mean.
